body:
> Is this worth specifying and making consistent across browsers?

In the past, we've shied away from constraining user interfaces. For example, you mention that you're only talking about desktop browsers; if we specified something desktop-specific, we'd be excluding mobile/watch/game console/etc. browsers. In some ways, standardization on desktop might make things worse for those other form factors, as it would encourage people to write desktop-only code!

It's possible we could write the specification as a kind of if-then constraint, e.g. "One possible interface is a textbox with two buttons. If you implement that interface, behave this way." Whether that's something we can do depends on whether browser vendors feel that such constraints on their future evolution would be helpful, or harmful.

As an example of how it might be unacceptable to some browsers, note that macOS has extremely different focus semantics than Windows and Linux, so we have not been able to specify specifics of focusability and focus movement.

I understand that constraining implementations could potentially limit progress. The exact behavior doesn't technically need to be specified here--I could just submit a patch to Firefox that changes the focus behavior to match Safari and Chrome. My concern is that there would be this de facto standard (interacting with a spinbox focuses it) that is required for web compatibility but not actually documented here, and if other browsers *do* come along and decide to implement their own bespoke input UI, they may miss out on that and break sites that expect certain focus semantics.

On the other hand, you already mentioned that you already don't want to specify focus semantics because they differ between OSes (what are macOS' focus semantics like? I don't own a machine that runs it sadly), so maybe it would be better to add a normative section warning developers not to rely on focus events being fired.

In general I'm not sure what particular freedom is afforded in practice by allowing browsers to implement their own UI elements in a way that they deem to be the best. Theoretically it allows for UI elements to be tailored for specific platforms/interaction models (desktop, mobile, console, etc), but in my experience, most sites/frameworks have come to rely on browsers implementing those UI elements in a specific way, and any attempt by browsers to redesign them will break those sites.

Most (all?) web frameworks have taken the route of eschewing native design guidelines in favor of creating their own, and while I'm not sure whether that's going to change in the future (`prefers-color-scheme` and the reintroduction of system colors in CSS Color Level 4 suggests a push to mimic native UI more, and the emergence of "reader mode" addons and browser features suggests that users may want something like that), it's a bit inconsistent in my mind to follow native design/interaction guidelines in these isolated pockets of `<input>` and the framework's guidelines on the rest of the page.
